title: Polynomial-time exact optimization of random asymmetric TSP
formal: Does there exist a uniform algorithm \(A\) and absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for the complete directed graph on \([n]\), with mutually independent costs \(w_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) for \(i\ne j\), the probability that \(A\) returns an exactly minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle within \(Cn^c\) arithmetic operations tends to one as \(n\to\infty\)? The algorithm must be correct whenever it terminates and terminate almost surely on this input distribution.
definitions:
For \(n\ge2\), the graph has every ordered edge \((i,j)\) with distinct endpoints. Opposite directions receive independent costs; no metric or triangle inequality is promised. A directed Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of all vertices, of cost \(\sum_{t=1}^n w_{v_t,v_{t+1}}\), where \(v_{n+1}=v_1\). Cyclic rotations represent the same tour. The optimum is the minimum of these finitely many sums. The output is a tour, not a rounded estimate of its value.

The explicit real-valued edge array is the input. Use a uniform real RAM with exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, nonzero division, comparisons, register accesses, ordinary indexing and optional fair random bits at unit cost. There is no unit-cost binary-digit extraction from a real. Exactness therefore means correctness of comparisons and of the chosen tour in this arithmetic model, rather than a claim about storing a continuously distributed input in finitely many bits.

Let \(T_A(w,\rho)\) be the operation count, allowing infinity for a nonterminating run, where \(\rho\) is an internal random tape independent of \(w\). Require zero-error output: every terminating run on an eligible edge array returns an optimum tour. Require \(\Pr[T_A<\infty]=1\) under the product input-and-coin law for each \(n\), and \(\Pr[T_A\le Cn^c]\to1\). Deterministic algorithms are included. Slow exceptional runs are allowed; a bound on expected runtime is not imposed. These conventions make the imported high-probability exact-computation question explicit.

The algorithm need not use branch and bound or any particular relaxation. The assignment relaxation permits several directed cycles instead of a single cycle; solving that relaxed problem exactly is not the same task. Likewise, an asymptotically negligible additive tour-cost error does not establish exact optimality.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated algorithmic existence and probability limit, or its logical negation in the specified arithmetic model. The proof must establish exact output correctness and one fixed polynomial runtime threshold holding with probability tending to one. A quasi-polynomial bound, approximate tours, or polynomial behavior only under a discrete small-integer cost distribution does not suffice. A lower bound for a particular branch-and-bound implementation does not refute the existence of all algorithms allowed here.
context:
Bell and Frieze study exact optimization under independent continuous costs. Version 15 states a high-probability runtime of exp((log n)^(2+o(1))), including uniform costs; this is quasi-polynomial, not a fixed polynomial.

Their historical discussion distinguishes near-optimal tours from exact optimization and discusses the longstanding polynomial-time branch-and-bound question. The present catalogue target permits any algorithm, so a positive branch-and-bound result would suffice but a negative result about that method alone would not.
why: This asks whether random instances remove the worst-case obstacle to exact asymmetric traveling-salesman optimization.

import_provenance.original_statement: When every directed edge of a complete graph receives an independent uniform[0,1] cost, can the minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle be found exactly in polynomial time with high probability? Bell–Frieze’s quasipolynomial-time algorithm leaves this central average-case algorithmic question open.
